title: Here's how to take the sting out of the cost of installing a heat pump
summary: Electrek (2024) on NREL's study: most households would see lower bills, but high install costs limit payoff; IRA rebates and credits help.

assertions.quote: 62% to 95% of households, depending upon heat pump efficiency – using a heat pump would see a drop in their energy bills.

verdicts.note: Bills rise in 39% of homes with minimum-efficiency units and 5% with cold-climate high-efficiency units, so a majority save in every scenario, though fewer than a third of gas homes do with minimum units.

Edwards' Monte Carlo model at 2020 prices finds 53% of households in its dataset would clearly see lower energy bills, against 19% higher and 28% unclear, a thin majority under conservative single-stage assumptions.

assertions.quote: For the 49 million homes that use electricity, fuel oil, or propane for heat and have AC, 92-100% of homes would see energy bill savings
natural gas prices are much lower than electricity prices on a BTU basis in many parts of the US.
Heat pumps may only be financially feasible for a smaller portion of households due to high installation costs.

verdicts.note: NREL's 2024 study found bill savings for most homes but positive net present value for far fewer once installation cost is counted.
Higher upfront costs cut positive unsubsidized NPV to 41% and 21% for the more efficient units despite bigger bill savings; cost reductions are needed for almost half of households.
Small reductions in capital cost could greatly increase economic adoption rates, which are limited to 21% of houses at current costs.
RMI finds gas customers face higher upfront retrofit costs, and in Houston and Oakland the energy savings are too small to make up the extra capital.

LBNL: even the cheapest deep path (heat pump electrification with PV and weatherization, about $54k) needed about $20k of cost cuts to break even monthly; this applies to whole retrofit packages, not a heat pump alone.
At $9,450 installed, a ccASHP with propane backup had a lifetime savings-to-investment ratio of 0.63 against a condensing furnace (does not pay off) but 1.24 against an 82% furnace.

In the UK the heat pump's net private cost after the grant is about £4,121 over 20 years on a standard tariff (it does not pay off), but switching to the heat pump time-of-use tariff is worth about £4,675, which more than covers it.
In some Canadian regions heat pumps win on lifetime cost only with current rebates and carbon pricing, especially under high upfront-cost assumptions, while elsewhere they win even without support.

assertions.quote: homeowners could “save thousands of dollars on average” by installing a smaller heat pump if they first improve their houses’ energy efficiency
There are Inflation Reduction Act rebates and tax credits to be had right now for heat pumps
households get a 30% tax credit for heat pumps and heat pump water heaters, capped at $2,000 per year
